label: Set Theory and Logic
notes: Open the chapter. Before topology proper we fix the language of sets, functions, and logic that every later argument relies on. The chapter reviews set operations, functions and relations, the integers and induction, countability, and the axiom of choice with the well-ordering theorem.

label: Sets and Functions
notes: Recall the basic set operations of union, intersection, difference, and complement, together with De Morgan's laws and arbitrary indexed families. A function is a rule with a domain and range; we distinguish injective, surjective, and bijective maps and study how images and preimages interact with unions and intersections, the workhorse facts of the subject.

label: Relations and Order
notes: Introduce relations as subsets of a product. Equivalence relations partition a set into classes, while order relations give comparisons. Linear orders, the order type of the integers and reals, and constructions like the dictionary order set up examples we will revisit when building order topologies on sets later in the course.

label: Integers and Induction
notes: Build the natural numbers and the principle of induction, then the well-ordering property that every nonempty set of positive integers has a least element. Recursive definitions are justified here. These tools let us define finite sets precisely and prove their basic combinatorial properties before passing to infinite sets.

label: Countable and Uncountable Sets
notes: Define a set as countable when it injects into the integers. Finite unions and countable unions of countable sets stay countable, and the rationals are countable. Cantor's diagonal argument shows the reals are uncountable, establishing a genuine hierarchy of infinite sizes that matters for many topological constructions.

label: Choice and Well-Ordering
notes: State the axiom of choice and its equivalents: Zorn's lemma and the well-ordering theorem. These principles let us select elements from infinitely many sets simultaneously and order any set. They are indispensable for results like Tychonoff's theorem, so we adopt them and note where they are used. Next: topological spaces.
